title: THEY CALLED HER A HARLOT. GOD WROTE HER INTO THE BLOODLINE OF JESUS CHRIST.
paragraphs: THEY CALLED HER A HARLOT. GOD WROTE HER INTO THE BLOODLINE OF JESUS CHRIST.

She lived in a condemned city, carried a reputation that could have destroyed her future, and had no claim to Israel’s promises. Yet when God wrote the earthly genealogy of His Son, Rahab’s name was there. Why would a holy God choose a woman with such a scandalous past? The answer may change how you see your own.
There is something almost unbearable about being remembered for the worst thing people know about you.
You can change your life. You can walk away from the darkness. You can spend years trying to become someone different.
But sometimes, people still introduce you to the world through the chapter you desperately wish they would stop reading.
The adulterer.
The addict.
The woman with a past.
The man who ruined his family.
The Christian who fell.
The person everybody whispers about.
And perhaps the most painful part is that some of those accusations are not entirely false.
You really did make those choices.
You really did cross those lines.
You really do have things in your history that you cannot undo.
So you learn to live with a terrible question quietly burning inside your chest.
Can God still do something beautiful with a life that has been so deeply stained?

If that question has ever followed you into the night, I want you to meet a woman whose name should make every self-righteous heart uncomfortable and every repentant sinner look toward heaven with hope.
Her name was Rahab.
And before we reach the end of her story, you will understand why her presence in the genealogy of Jesus Christ is not an embarrassing detail the Bible forgot to remove.
It is a breathtaking testimony to the kind of Savior Jesus came to be.
Because Rahab was not born into Israel.
She was a Canaanite woman living in Jericho, a city standing under the judgment of God.
And Scripture does not introduce her with an impressive family background, a spotless reputation, or a record of religious accomplishments.
Joshua 2:1 identifies her with a Hebrew word that makes modern readers uncomfortable.
זוֹנָה — zonah.
A prostitute.
Not merely a misunderstood woman with an unfair nickname. Not simply an innkeeper whose occupation was accidentally mistranslated.
The Hebrew text uses a word ordinarily associated with prostitution, and the New Testament preserves that identification.
Hebrews 11:31 calls her Rahab the prostitute.
James 2:25 does the same.
The Bible does not sanitize her past to make her redemption easier for respectable people to accept.
And that matters.
Because if we rewrite Rahab into someone who never needed grace, we lose the very beauty of what God did in her life.
But notice something equally important.
Scripture identifies her occupation without telling us every circumstance that brought her there.
We are not told whether poverty, exploitation, personal choices, or some combination of painful realities shaped her life.
We are not given permission to invent the details.
What we know is enough.
She was a woman with a stigmatized occupation, living among a people facing divine judgment, with no obvious reason to expect that her name would someday appear in the family history of the Messiah.
Yet it did.
And that is where this story becomes astonishing.
Imagine Jericho before the walls fell.
A fortified city.
Heavy gates.
Watchful soldiers.
Families preparing meals.
Merchants conducting business.
People laughing, arguing, planning weddings, and making promises about tomorrow.
Life continuing as though judgment could never arrive.
But something was happening beyond those walls.
Israel had crossed through the wilderness and was approaching the land God had promised.
The inhabitants of Jericho had heard the reports.
They knew about the Red Sea.
They knew what had happened to the Amorite kings.
They knew Israel's God was not merely another tribal deity to be dismissed.
And somewhere inside that city, a woman named Rahab was listening.
Joshua 2 tells us that Joshua sent two spies to examine the land, especially Jericho.
They entered Rahab's house.
When the king of Jericho learned that Israelite men had come there, he sent orders demanding that she surrender them.
Suddenly, Rahab faced a decision that could cost her everything.
She could protect herself by turning the spies over.
Or she could place herself in danger by protecting men who belonged to the people of Israel.
She chose to hide them.
And before anyone turns this into a simplistic lesson about deception, we need to be careful with the biblical text.

Rahab did mislead the king's messengers about the spies' whereabouts. Scripture reports what she did, while Hebrews and James commend her faith and her reception of the messengers. The passages do not require us to conclude that every element of her conduct was morally perfect.
The greater issue was the allegiance taking shape in her heart.
Rahab had begun to recognize something that many people with far more religious advantages still refuse to acknowledge.
The God of Israel was truly God.
Listen to what she told the spies.
In Joshua 2:11, Rahab declared:
"For the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath." (KJV)
Now look at the Hebrew behind that confession.
יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם הוּא אֱלֹהִים בַּשָּׁמַיִם מִמַּעַל וְעַל־הָאָרֶץ מִתָּחַת
YHWH eloheikhem hu Elohim bashamayim mimma'al ve'al-ha'arets mittachat.
A faithful rendering is:
"The LORD your God, He is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath."
This was not a vague acknowledgment that some supernatural power might exist.
Rahab confessed the supremacy of the LORD, the covenant God of Israel.
The Hebrew divine name, represented by the four consonants YHWH and traditionally rendered "LORD" in many English Bibles, identifies the God whose mighty acts she had heard about.
And here is what should stop us in our tracks.
Rahab had heard about God's power.
But she did not merely tremble before that power.
She responded by seeking mercy.
That is the difference between being frightened by the consequences of sin and turning toward the God who alone can save.
Many people fear exposure.
Many fear punishment.
Many fear losing relationships, reputation, or comfort.
But fear alone is not the same as saving faith.
Rahab's confession was joined to action.
She placed her safety in the hands of the God she had come to recognize as sovereign.
And then she made a request that reveals something deeply human about her.
She asked that her father, mother, brothers, sisters, and their households be spared.
Think about that.
A woman whose reputation could have caused others to dismiss her was pleading for the lives of her family.
The Bible does not tell us how her family treated her.
It does not describe their relationships.
But it does tell us that when Rahab sought deliverance, she wanted them delivered too.
Her concern reached beyond herself.
And I wonder how many people reading this understand that feeling.
You are asking God to rescue you.
But you are also carrying the names of people you love.
A son who no longer prays.
A daughter who has walked away from the faith.
A husband who seems spiritually unreachable.
A wife whose heart has grown cold.
Parents who have never surrendered to Christ.
A brother or sister whose life is unraveling.
You know what it means to look at your own need for mercy and still whisper:
"Lord, please remember my family too."
Rahab did not ask for a trophy.
She did not ask for wealth.
She asked for life.
And the spies agreed to spare her household under the conditions of their oath.
Then came the sign.
A scarlet cord.
Joshua 2:18 records their instruction that Rahab tie a scarlet cord in the window through which she had let them escape.
The Hebrew expression is:
תִּקְוַת חוּט הַשָּׁנִי
Tiqvat chut hashani.
In context, this refers to a cord or line of scarlet thread.
It was a visible sign identifying the house that was to be spared.
The people seeking protection were to remain inside, and Rahab was not to disclose the spies' mission.
When the walls of Jericho eventually fell, Joshua instructed the spies to bring Rahab and her family out, honoring the oath they had made.
Joshua 6:25 tells us that Rahab and her household were spared and that she came to dwell among Israel.
Read that again.
The woman who had lived inside a city marked for destruction was brought out alive.
The outsider was received among the people of Israel.
The woman who had been known as a prostitute was no longer defined only by the life she had lived in Jericho.
But there is a detail we must handle faithfully.
Some Christian teachers identify Rahab's scarlet cord as a direct prophecy of the blood of Jesus Christ.
The red color certainly invites a powerful Christian comparison with redemption through Christ's blood.
Yet Joshua does not explicitly say that the cord itself was a prophecy of the crucifixion.
Its immediate meaning was the sign of the spies' promise to spare her household.
We can recognize a beautiful theological parallel without claiming more than Scripture actually says.
The scarlet cord marked a household that would be spared in Jericho.
The blood of Jesus Christ accomplishes something infinitely greater.
It reconciles sinners to God.
It secures forgiveness through His sacrifice.
It opens the way to eternal life for everyone who truly trusts Him.
As 1 Peter 1:18–19 teaches, believers are redeemed not with perishable silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
Rahab's cord did not save the world.
Jesus did.
And that distinction makes the Gospel more glorious, not less.
But the story does not end with Rahab walking out of Jericho.
It becomes even more extraordinary hundreds of years later.
Open Matthew chapter 1.
Most people approach biblical genealogies the way they approach a long list of unfamiliar names.
They skim.
They skip.
They hurry toward the story they think matters.
But hidden inside Matthew's genealogy is a sentence that should make you stop reading and stare at the page.
Matthew 1:5 says:
"And Salmon begat Booz of Rachab; and Booz begat Obed of Ruth; and Obed begat Jesse." (KJV)
The spelling "Booz" is the older English form of Boaz.
And "Rachab" is Rahab.
The Greek text includes these remarkable words:
Σαλμὼν δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Βόες ἐκ τῆς Ῥαχάβ
Salmon de egennēsen ton Boes ek tēs Rhachab.
Meaning:
"And Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab."
There it is.
Not a rumor.
Not a medieval legend.
Not a sentimental invention designed to make a sermon more dramatic.
Matthew names Rahab in the genealogy that leads to Jesus Christ.
According to Matthew's account, Rahab was the mother of Boaz.
Boaz became the father of Obed through Ruth.
Obed became the father of Jesse.
Jesse became the father of David.
And through the royal line of David, Matthew traces the ancestry of Jesus, the promised Messiah.
Pause and consider the staggering beauty of that.
Rahab had once been a woman living behind the walls of Jericho.
Now her name stood inside the family history of Israel's greatest King and, ultimately, the Messiah.
The woman once associated with prostitution was remembered in Scripture as an ancestor of Jesus.
And Matthew did not hide her.
He named her.
Why?
Because the genealogy of Jesus is not a public-relations campaign designed to make His human ancestry look impressive.
It is a testimony to the faithfulness of God across generations of deeply imperfect human beings.
Matthew includes Tamar.
He includes Rahab.
He includes Ruth.
He refers to the wife of Uriah, Bathsheba, in a way that recalls David's grievous sin.
These women have different stories, and we should not pretend their circumstances or moral responsibilities were identical.
Ruth, for example, is presented as a woman of remarkable loyalty and faithfulness, not as someone with Rahab's former occupation.
But their presence together reveals something significant.
God's redemptive purposes were not restricted to the socially powerful, the ethnically privileged, or those whose family histories appeared uncomplicated.
The promised Messiah entered human history through a family line that included outsiders, broken situations, grievous sins, courageous faith, and astonishing mercy.
Jesus did not inherit personal sin from His ancestors.
Scripture is clear that Christ Himself was without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
His holiness was not compromised by the moral failures found in His earthly genealogy.
Rather, His genealogy shows the extraordinary faithfulness of God in bringing the sinless Savior into a sinful world.
And this is where Rahab's story begins to confront us personally.
Because we often assume God works the way human beings do.
We think He looks for impressive résumés.
We think He prefers spotless backgrounds.
We think He must be reluctant to associate Himself with people who have embarrassing histories.
We imagine that our past has the final authority to determine our future.
But Rahab's story dismantles that assumption.
She was not rescued because prostitution was harmless.
She was not included in the Messiah's genealogy because sin does not matter.
She was not honored because repentance is unnecessary.
She was spared in the context of a genuine response of faith, and the New Testament holds her up as an example of faith that acted.
Hebrews 11:31 declares:
"By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace." (KJV)
The Greek begins:
Πίστει Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη
Pistei Rhaab hē pornē.
"By faith, Rahab the prostitute..."
That opening is extraordinary.
The Greek word πίστει (pistei) means "by faith."
The writer of Hebrews does not pretend her past never existed.
He places her among the examples of faith.
And James 2:25 points to her actions as evidence of that faith.
This is crucial.
Rahab was not saved by an impressive record of good works.
Nor was her faith merely a private opinion that changed nothing about her behavior.
She believed, and her allegiance became visible in what she did.
James uses her example to demonstrate that living faith is not empty religious talk.
True faith bears fruit.
And that leads us to a question more important than whether people still remember your past.
Has your faith in Jesus Christ begun to change the direction of your life?
Not whether you have become perfect.
Not whether you have erased every consequence of yesterday.
Not whether everyone has forgiven you.
But whether you have truly turned toward Christ.
Because grace is not God's permission to remain enslaved to sin.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that saves us and begins transforming us.
Ephesians 2:8–10 holds these truths together.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Forgiveness is not something we purchase through moral improvement.
Obedience is not the price we pay to make Jesus love us.
But when His grace truly takes hold of a life, it does not leave that life untouched.
Somebody needs to hear that.
Especially the person who has been using shame as an excuse to stay away from God.
You tell yourself that you will pray when you become better.
You will return to church when you feel worthy.
You will open your Bible when your habits are under control.
You will surrender when you have finally cleaned up the mess.
But if you could cleanse your own soul, you would not need a Savior.
Jesus did not come because humanity needed a little religious encouragement.
He came because sinners needed redemption.
He lived without sin.
He died for our sins.
He was buried.
And He rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
The cross is not a decorative symbol for people who have already made themselves acceptable.
It is the place where the holy Son of God gave Himself for sinners who could never save themselves.
And the resurrection is the declaration that death does not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
That is why Rahab's story matters.
Not because everyone with a painful past will become famous.
Not because faith guarantees that every damaged relationship will be repaired immediately.
Not because following God removes all earthly consequences.
And certainly not because God owes us an impressive future if we make one courageous decision.
Rahab's place in Jesus' genealogy was a particular gift within God's unfolding plan of redemption.
We should not turn it into a universal promise that every believer will receive public recognition or extraordinary earthly success.
The deeper promise is better.
Through Jesus Christ, sinners can receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and a new life that their past cannot purchase or prevent.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired everything.
Not after everyone approved of us.
Not after our reputations became respectable.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
That truth should break the pride of the religious and lift the eyes of the ashamed.
Because there are two ways to misunderstand Rahab.
One is to despise her because of her former life.
The other is to romanticize her former life as though sin itself were the reason she was honored.
Neither understands grace.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace reveals a Savior whose mercy is greater than the guilt of those who turn to Him.
And perhaps that is why this genealogy feels so personal.
Some of us have lived through our own Jericho.
Not a literal Canaanite fortress, but a life surrounded by walls of secrecy, regret, fear, addiction, bitterness, compromise, or spiritual rebellion.
We built those walls to protect ourselves.
We learned how to smile while hiding the truth.
We became skilled at looking normal.
We posted the family pictures.
We attended the worship services.
We said, "I'm blessed," while quietly fighting battles nobody knew existed.
And somewhere inside, we wondered whether God could see the person behind the performance.
He can.
He sees the hidden sin that needs repentance.
He sees the wounds that need healing.
He sees the pride that needs surrender.
He sees the fear beneath the anger.
He sees the exhaustion behind the smile.
And He calls us not to manufacture a better disguise, but to come into the light.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Notice that the promise does not say we should pretend we never sinned.
It calls us to confess.
To stop defending what God calls evil.
To stop making peace with what is destroying us.
To come honestly before the Lord.
Perhaps your first step today is not to write a long explanation of why you became the person you are.
Perhaps it is simply to say:
"Jesus, I have sinned. I cannot save myself. I believe You died and rose again. Have mercy on me. Teach me to follow You."
That prayer is not a magical formula.
The saving power belongs to Jesus Christ, not to the precise arrangement of our words.
But genuine repentance and faith are never wasted on Him.
And if you are already a believer who has stumbled badly, do not mistake the pain of conviction for proof that God has no more mercy for you.
Come back to the truth.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Seek forgiveness where you have caused harm.
Make restitution where it is appropriate and possible.
Seek wise pastoral counsel and accountability when needed.
Turn away from the sin that has been consuming your life.
Do not use grace to hide from responsibility.
Let grace give you the courage to face it.
And remember Rahab.
Not as permission to keep living in Jericho.
But as a witness that God can receive someone who turns to Him in faith.
There is another detail in her story that deserves our attention.
Rahab did not simply escape a burning chapter of her past.
She became part of a community.
Joshua 6:25 says she lived among Israel.
Her story moved from separation to belonging.
And that is one reason Christianity was never meant to be lived as an isolated private experience.
We need Scripture.
We need prayer.
We need sound teaching.
We need fellowship.
We need believers who will encourage us when we are weary and lovingly confront us when we are drifting.
We need a community that does not confuse holiness with pretending.
A community where repentance is taken seriously, forgiveness is celebrated, and Jesus remains at the center.
That is also the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
Not to build a following around human personalities.
Not to sell people the illusion that spiritual growth can be purchased.
Not to replace the local church or the shepherding of faithful Christian leaders.
But to help place biblical truth, Christian encouragement, and discipleship resources within reach of people who need to hear about Jesus Christ.
These resources are offered to encourage deeper study, spiritual growth, and a more faithful walk with the Lord.
Perhaps there is a struggling believer who has almost stopped praying.
Perhaps there is a young person who has never been taught how to read Scripture carefully.
Perhaps there is someone who feels too ashamed to walk into a church building but is willing to read one article about the mercy of Jesus.
Think of it as a voluntary monthly ministry offering—an expression of generosity that helps continue and expand this work.
Your money does not purchase God's favor.
But supporting faithful Christian ministry can be one meaningful way to honor Him, serve others, and participate in the work of making the Gospel known.
If Gospel Warrior has helped you grow closer to Christ, and you believe in the mission, we would be grateful to have you stand with us.
Those products are simply an additional expression of appreciation.
The greater purpose is the ministry itself.
More Scripture shared.
More discipleship resources made available.
More people encouraged to seek Christ.
More opportunities to point weary hearts toward the Savior.
Keep reading.
Keep studying.
Keep praying.
Keep growing.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And neither is the love of Jesus.
There is another powerful way you can help.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
But because somebody in your circle may be carrying a shame they have never spoken aloud.
Somebody may be convinced that the worst thing they ever did is the only thing God sees when He looks at them.
Somebody may have abandoned prayer because they think heaven has stopped listening.
And perhaps, through a simple act of sharing, they will encounter the biblical testimony of a woman named Rahab and discover that the door of mercy is not closed to repentant sinners.
And if this story has touched a place in your heart that you usually keep hidden, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
You do not need to reveal private details or expose wounds you are not ready to discuss publicly.
And if you need prayer, simply write:
Let the comments become a place where people encourage one another with Scripture, compassion, truth, and prayer rather than judgment or spectacle.
For the nights when your past seems louder than God's promises.
For the moments when you need to remember that biblical grace does not deny sin, but points sinners to the Savior.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, those who have grown spiritually cold, and even those who do not yet believe in Jesus to join us.
Because the goal is not merely to collect followers.
It is to help people become faithful followers of Jesus.
But before you leave, I want you to return to that ancient city one final time.
Picture Rahab at her window.
The scarlet cord is there.
The city is facing judgment.
She has heard what the LORD has done.
She has confessed who He is.
She has acted in faith.
She does not know the full story of what her life will become.
She does not know that generations later, a Jewish tax collector named Matthew will write a Gospel account tracing the ancestry of the Messiah.
She does not know that her name will be read by believers across nations and centuries.
She does not know that people wrestling with shame thousands of years later will find encouragement in her testimony.
All she knows is that the God of Israel is truly God, and she has sought mercy from Him.
Then the walls fall.
But Rahab lives.
Years pass.
Generations come and go.
A son named Boaz enters the family story.
Then Obed.
Then Jesse.
Then David.
And much later, in Bethlehem, Jesus Christ is born.
The promised Son of David.
The Son of Abraham.
The Savior who would bear the sins of many.
The One who would welcome repentant sinners, confront the proud, heal the broken, call people out of darkness, and give His life as a ransom for many.
The One who would rise from the grave.
The One before whom every knee will bow.
And there, in the opening chapter of Matthew's Gospel, is Rahab's name.
Not because her past was righteous.
Not because her faith made her worthy of every blessing.
Not because her story was free from complications.
But because God, in His sovereign faithfulness, chose to include this woman of faith in the earthly ancestry of His Son.
The scandal did not become the center of her story.
God's grace did.
And now we can answer the question that brought us here.
Why did Rahab, a Canaanite woman with a troubled reputation, become part of Jesus' genealogy?
Because God was accomplishing His redemptive purposes through real human history, showing that His mercy reaches beyond the boundaries people often assume are permanent.
Because Rahab responded to the revelation of the LORD with faith that became visible through her actions.
Because she was received among Israel, and Matthew records her place in the family line leading to the Messiah.
And because her inclusion helps us see something essential about the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come into a world of morally spotless people who had no need of salvation.
He came into our world.
A world of sin and sorrow.
Of pride and betrayal.
Of broken families and wounded hearts.
Of people who need more than advice.
People who need redemption.
And through His sinless life, sacrificial death, and victorious resurrection, He provides the salvation no human ancestry, reputation, religious achievement, or personal effort could ever secure.
That is why the story of Rahab is not ultimately about celebrating Rahab.
It is about magnifying the God who showed her mercy and fulfilled His promises through Jesus Christ.
And that is why your story does not have to end where your sin began.
You may not be able to change what happened yesterday.
You may not be able to make everyone forget.
You may still have consequences to face, relationships to repair, and difficult steps of obedience ahead.
But if you turn to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith, you are not asking a reluctant Savior to consider helping you.
You are coming to the One who gave Himself to save sinners.
The One whose grace is not fragile.
The One whose forgiveness is not earned.
The One who does not need to falsify your history in order to redeem your life.
So come to Him.
Not with excuses.
Not with a carefully edited version of yourself.
Not with the belief that you must first become worthy.
Come with the truth.
Come with repentance.
Come with faith.
And let the Savior who died and rose again have the final word over your eternal future.
Because the most extraordinary thing about Rahab is not that a woman with a scandalous past appeared in the genealogy of Jesus.
It is that Jesus, the holy Son of God, came to save people with scandalous pasts—and people with respectable appearances who are just as desperately in need of grace.
The world may remember the name they gave you in your darkest chapter, but in Christ, that chapter does not have to be the ending of your story.
